clue.text: It's framed to gain money, we hear

indicators.note: the phrase tells the solver the words are to be taken as spoken, so a sound-alike is wanted

parts.note: to gain money is to win dough, dough being slang for cash

explanation.surface: Someone is setting something up, perhaps a scam, to make a profit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' is a link. Said out loud, WIN DOUGH sounds like the answer, and 'we hear' signals the sound-alike.
explanation.definitionFit: A pane of glass is set in a frame in the wall, so the opening for light is something framed.

clue.text: Jonson honoured. Shakespeare's memory on this side —

definitions.text: Jonson honoured. Shakespeare's memory on this side —

parts.words: Jonson honoured. Shakespeare's memory on this side —
parts.note: Ben Jonson wrote that he honoured Shakespeare's memory on this side of excessive worship; the missing word completes his quotation

explanation.surface: A fill-in-the-blank quotation from Ben Jonson about Shakespeare.
explanation.walkthrough: Jonson wrote 'I loved the man, and do honour his memory, on this side idolatry, as much as any'.
explanation.definitionFit: The worship of images or false gods, used of excessive admiration for a person.

clue.text: Fixed propeller on it in the river.

indicators.note: the propeller and it are placed inside the river

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Scotland and another in Wales and England
a fish propels itself with a fin
the word as written

explanation.surface: A propeller was fastened into place on a boat in the river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is a link setting FIN beside IT.
explanation.definitionFit: Something settled or certain is fixed, as a fixed date is a set date.

clue.text: Where clearing banks will help-a horseman

definitions.text: Where clearing banks will help-a horseman

parts.words: Where clearing banks will help-a horseman
parts.note: clearing banks suggests the big high-street banks, but here it means a horse clearing the banks of a ditch at a steeplechase

explanation.surface: Sounds like a high-street bank offering a rider a loan.
explanation.walkthrough: Clearing banks are British high-street banks that clear cheques; here a horse clears the banks of water.
explanation.definitionFit: A fence with a ditch of water beyond it, jumped in steeplechases.

clue.text: Underground explorer, or golfer putting for championship ?

explanation.surface: A caver, or perhaps a golfer on the green with a title at stake.
explanation.definitionFit: A caver explores pots (deep caves); a golfer putting tries to sink, or pot, the ball in the hole.

clue.text: Did revellers do so, to give Petra its description ?

definitions.text: Did revellers do so, to give Petra its description ?

parts.words: Did revellers do so, to give Petra its description ?
parts.note: Petra is the rose-red city half as old as time; revellers going wild on a night out suggest colouring a whole city

explanation.surface: Asks whether party-goers gave the ancient city of Petra its colour.
explanation.walkthrough: Burgon's poem calls Petra 'a rose-red city half as old as time'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to go out celebrating wildly; literally it would colour a city crimson.

clue.text: For' farmworkers it's the limit in the small hours

indicators.note: the limit is placed inside the abbreviation for hours

parts.note: hrs is the short form of hours, so small hours means hours shortened
an edge is a boundary or limit

explanation.surface: Farm labourers find it all too much in the early morning.
explanation.definitionFit: Farmhands who trim and lay field boundaries of shrubs are named for that work.

clue.text: Lottie upset about some lines in the book of words

indicators.note: the scrambled name goes around the lines, with them inside
upset means knocked over or disordered, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: BR is British Rail, which ran railway lines

explanation.surface: Lottie is upset by some lines in a script.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' rearranges LOTTIE into LIETTO, which goes 'about' BR (British Rail, a crossword stock for lines).
explanation.definitionFit: The text of an opera or musical is its words, printed as a booklet.

clue.text: Hopeful state achieved by those who 5 dn ?

definitions.text: Hopeful state achieved by those who 5 dn ?

parts.words: Hopeful state achieved by those who 5 dn ?
parts.note: revellers who make a city crimson, as in 5 down, would turn pinkish; the same word is used for optimism

explanation.surface: Asks what optimistic frame of mind wild revellers reach.
explanation.definitionFit: Optimism is a rose-tinted outlook, and pinkness of colour shares the word.

clue.text: Papers aimed to cover no single departure

definitions.text: Papers aimed to cover no single departure

parts.words: Papers aimed to cover no single departure
parts.note: scraps of paper are thrown over a couple leaving their wedding: they are no longer single as they depart

explanation.surface: Documents meant to deal with a departure that is not a solo one.
explanation.definitionFit: Small paper pieces are thrown at newly married couples as they leave the ceremony.

clue.text: We have, trouble with less than-best bricks

parts.note: ado is fuss or trouble, as in much ado about nothing

indicators.note: less than the full word, so its final letter is dropped from the word best

parts.note: the word as written

explanation.surface: Builders complain about having to work with second-rate bricks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'We have' is a link. 'less-than' cuts the final T off BEST, leaving BES.
explanation.definitionFit: Sun-dried mud bricks used in hot countries go by this Spanish name.

clue.text: Knight's. diminutive flag?

explanation.surface: A small pennant belonging to a knight.
explanation.definitionFit: A knight banneret led men under his own banner; and the -et ending makes a little flag, a small pennant.

clue.text: This the first Labour lion

parts.note: Hercules' first labour was to kill the lion of a valley in the Peloponnese; the lion is not a party politician

explanation.surface: Reads like praise for a leading figure of the Labour Party.
explanation.walkthrough: Labour suggests the British political party; it is one of the twelve labours of Hercules, the first of which was slaying a lion.
explanation.definitionFit: The lion Hercules strangled in his first labour came from the valley of Nemea in Greece.

clue.text: Contact-men scour the possibility — of loans ?

explanation.surface: Agents look into whether credit can be raised.
explanation.definitionFit: People who touch are in physical contact; in slang, to touch someone is to ask them for a loan.

clue.text: You'll get a change of heart, girl, in the back of the car

definitions.text: in the back of the car

indicators.note: a change of the letters means they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A girl changing her mind while sitting in the back seat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You'll get a' is a link. 'change of' rearranges HEART and GIRL together.
explanation.definitionFit: The red lamp at the tail of a vehicle sits at its back.

clue.text: Chain dance, say

indicators.note: say asks the solver to speak the word, so a sound-alike is in play

parts.note: the jive is a lively jazz-age dance

explanation.surface: A conga line, perhaps.
explanation.definitionFit: A gyve is an old word for a fetter or shackle, so to chain is to fetter.

clue.text: Gladstone backed Harrow with no quarter given for this wicked place

parts.note: Gladstone was nicknamed the GOM, the Grand Old Man

indicators.note: a quarter is a compass point, here W, which is left out

parts.note: the word as written

explanation.surface: The Victorian prime minister supported Harrow School ruthlessly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backed' turns HARROW into WORRAH; 'with no quarter given' drops W (west, a compass quarter), leaving ORRAH. Harrow is a famous English public school.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical city destroyed with Sodom for its sinfulness.

clue.text: Hampden in Stoke Poges

parts.note: Gray's Elegy, set in Stoke Poges churchyard, mentions some village Hampden buried there

explanation.surface: Names the politician John Hampden in a Buckinghamshire village.
explanation.walkthrough: Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard, set at Stoke Poges, speaks of 'some village-Hampden', a local resident.
explanation.definitionFit: A rustic local resident: Gray's humble man who might have been a Hampden lived in a small rural community.

clue.text: Fair ones being (made by) policewomen

parts.note: an arrest is a cop, as in it's a fair cop; and police officers of either sex

explanation.surface: Women officers making blonde arrests, or being blonde themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's a fair cop' is the classic British phrase a caught criminal uses, admitting the arrest is deserved.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for police officers, and also for arrests, as in a fair arrest admitted by the culprit.

clue.text: Party's plays on words

parts.note: a parlour game at parties acts out words syllable by syllable

explanation.surface: Puns made at a party.
explanation.definitionFit: A party game where players act out the syllables of a word for others to guess.

clue.text: H.M.S. dressed overall ?

parts.note: a ship dressed overall has flags strung from stem to stern; Gilbert and Sullivan's naval operetta is named after an apron-like garment

explanation.surface: A Royal Navy ship decked out with flags.
explanation.walkthrough: Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera is H.M.S. Pinafore.
explanation.definitionFit: A sleeveless apron dress worn over clothes is a kind of overall.

clue.text: Decimal money, down?

parts.note: a decimal point is a dot, and money paid down is paid at once

explanation.surface: A question about whether decimal currency has lost value.
explanation.definitionFit: Payment made immediately, cash on the nail; the point in a decimal number is also a dot.

clue.text: Students' union put up increase early in the day

indicators.note: in a down clue, put up means read from bottom to top

parts.note: NUS is the National Union of Students
a rise is an increase

explanation.surface: The students' union has raised its subscription early in the day.
explanation.definitionFit: Dawn comes at the start of the morning.

clue.text: Former pupil not short of the figure

parts.note: OB stands for old boy, a former pupil of a school
the opposite of short is long

explanation.surface: An old boy who is slim, or someone not short of the right shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A rectangle longer than it is wide is a geometric shape of this name.

clue.text: Having studied in, depth?

parts.note: a well is deep, so to read in depth suggests reading at the bottom of a well

explanation.surface: Someone who has researched a subject thoroughly.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who has done much reading is knowledgeable and widely studied.

clue.text: Get: back in gear, anyway

indicators.note: any way of arranging the letters will do, so the words are mixed up

explanation.surface: A driver putting the car back into gear somehow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyway' tells you to rearrange IN and GEAR.
explanation.definitionFit: To recover something lost is to obtain it again.

clue.text: Capital party on. Dance ?

parts.note: Riga is the capital of Latvia
a do is a party or celebration
the word as written

explanation.surface: A big party in the capital goes on: is there dancing?
explanation.definitionFit: An old lively court dance for couples, of Provençal origin.

clue.text: He'd go around the forest unimpressed

indicators.note: the letters of he'd encircle the forest, going around it

parts.note: the word as written with its apostrophe dropped
the Forest of Arden is the setting of As You Like It

explanation.surface: A man would walk round the woods without being impressed.
explanation.walkthrough: ARDEN is the Warwickshire forest in Shakespeare's As You Like It.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone toughened by experience is no longer moved or impressed by things.

clue.text: Sampler placed over the bed

explanation.surface: An embroidered sampler hung above the bed.
explanation.definitionFit: One who tries things out is a trier; also a canopy above a four-poster bed bears this name.
